What ΔE means here — and why CMYK can't hit every Pantone
ΔE2000 is one number for how different two colors look — here, the Pantone target vs. the closest CMYK build on this material. Rough guide: <1 imperceptible · 1–2 very close (only visible side-by-side) · 2–3 a solid commercial match · 3–6 noticeable, often still acceptable · >6 clearly different (flagged).

What ΔE is not: it isn't an automatic pass/fail — acceptable tolerance depends on the color, the customer, and whether it's a critical brand color. A flagged ΔE doesn't mean the print is bad; it means the Pantone lives outside what four inks can mix, so you're seeing the nearest achievable color.

Why the gaps exist: Pantone spot colors are premixed inks (Pantone/X-Rite base inks) formulated to hit one exact color — including many outside the CMYK gamut entirely: saturated oranges, greens, blues, purples, and anything neon. Process CMYK reaches only a portion of the library — commonly cited as roughly half, and fewer at tight tolerance. PANTONE Reflex Blue C is the classic miss: no CMYK mix gets there.

These numbers are predicted from your media ICC profile, with targets from your PrintFactory CxF (D50/2°). The final step is to print a Pantone chart, measure each patch M2 on the Barbieri, and replace predicted ΔE with measured — then this viewer reflects exactly what your press does.
